items.title: Bartlett showed memory reconstructs around schemas
items.claim: Frederic Bartlett's 1932 'War of the Ghosts' study asked British participants to recall a Native American folk tale. What pattern emerged?

options.text: Participants progressively rationalised the story to fit British cultural schemas — omitting culturally unfamiliar elements, shortening, replacing 'canoes' with 'boats' — demonstrating reconstructive memory

items.reveal:
Bartlett's 'Remembering' (1932) introduced 'schemas' to cognitive psychology. Participants' recall after weeks or months showed systematic distortions consistent with making the story 'make sense' in their own cultural framework.

Methodological critics note Bartlett's loose instructions and lack of statistical analysis. The schema concept has been operationalised more rigorously since (Brewer & Treyens 1981 office study; Loftus on eyewitness memory).
items.why: Memory is not playback. The same mechanism that lets us remember efficiently makes us systematically misremember in predictable ways.

items.title: The magical number seven
items.claim: George Miller's 1956 paper proposed a famous limit on short-term memory. What was the span?
items.reveal:
Miller's 1956 paper 'The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two' described short-term memory span as roughly 5 to 9 items.

Later work by Cowan (2001) revised the effective limit to around 4 chunks once rehearsal is controlled.
items.why: Capacity depends on how information is grouped. Chunking effectively expands what fits in working memory.

items.title: Long-term memory is not one system
items.claim: Endel Tulving distinguished episodic and semantic memory. What is the key difference?

options.text: Episodic stores facts; semantic stores experiences

Episodic memory is autobiographical and time-stamped (your breakfast this morning); semantic is general knowledge (London is the UK capital). Procedural memory (how to ride a bike) is a third, separate system

items.reveal:
Patient HM (Henry Molaison) could not form new episodic memories after his 1953 surgery but retained semantic knowledge from before the operation and could acquire new procedural skills (motor mirror-tracing).

Neuroimaging (Tulving, Nyberg, Cabeza 2000s) supports differential activation: hippocampus crucial for episodic; widespread cortical networks for semantic; basal ganglia/cerebellum for procedural. Different forms of dementia (semantic dementia vs Alzheimer's) damage these systems differently.
items.why: Treating memory as a single capacity misses clinically and educationally important distinctions. Memory loss patterns reveal architecture.
